soil-found-030.title: Eight elements and the swaps that multiply minerals
soil-found-030.text: Just eight elements make up over 98% of the Earth's crust by weight. In decreasing order they are oxygen, silicon, aluminum, iron, magnesium, calcium, sodium and potassium. Oxygen alone forms 47% and silicon 28%. Mineral chemistry explains how this supply, and the swapping of one ion for another, decides which minerals exist and how varied they are. The minerals that form are those most stable at the temperature and pressure of formation, within the limits set by the rock's overall chemistry. Ions substitute for one another only when close in size and charge. Al3+ commonly replaces Si4+, since the two are similar in charge, size and crustal abundance. In the silicon–oxygen minerals of {{ref:soil-found-031}}, that swap leaves a charge to balance. This is why so many different minerals of that family exist. Change a rock's composition, by weathering or by hydrothermal alteration, and its minerals change with it.

soil-found-035.title: Oxide minerals, where oxygen holds the metals
soil-found-035.text: The world's chief aluminum ore is a product of extreme weathering. This ore, {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, is a mixture of hydroxides that forms where chemical weathering is very intense. It belongs to the oxide minerals, those in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, or negatively charged ion. They fall into three groups: simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides. Corundum (Al2O3) and the iron oxide Fe2O3, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, belong to the corundum group of simple oxides. Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two oxidation states, Fe2+ and Fe3+. Oxides also form during weathering. Water converts many primary minerals to fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides through the reactions described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}.

soil-found-037.title: The handful of minerals that build most rock
soil-found-037.text: Thousands of mineral species exist, but a few do most of the building. Rock-forming minerals are the species and groups far more abundant in rocks than the rest. The main ones are quartz, the feldspars, micas, amphiboles, pyroxenes, olivines and calcite. All but calcite are silicates. A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids. Some rocks are mostly one mineral: limestone is calcite and quartzite is quartz. Others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals. Rocks need not be mineral at all. Coal is a sedimentary rock made mainly of organically derived carbon.

soil-found-031.title: Silicates: one building block, many ways to link it
soil-found-031.text: Approximately 90% of the Earth's crust is silicate minerals, and all of them share one building block. It is the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, a silicon atom surrounded by four oxygens. Silicon almost always sits in this four-fold, tetrahedral arrangement with oxygen. What varies is how the tetrahedra link. They polymerize, or join up, to different degrees, and mineralogists group silicates by that degree. At one end are isolated tetrahedra, the orthosilicates. Then come paired tetrahedra, rings and chains. Single-chain silicates are mostly pyroxenes, which make up about 10% of the crust. Double-chain silicates are often amphiboles. Next come two-dimensional sheets, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-033}}. At the far end are three-dimensional frameworks sharing all four corners, the tectosilicates of {{ref:soil-found-032}}. One substitution adds variety. Al3+ often replaces Si4+ in the tetrahedra, because the two ions have similar radius and charge. The swap changes how the structure's charge must be balanced, as {{ref:soil-found-030}} showed.

soil-found-032.title: Quartz and feldspar, the sturdy framework silicates
soil-found-032.text: Quartz is the most abundant mineral species, making up 12% of the crust. It belongs to the framework silicates, whose tetrahedra share all four corners. This is the most polymerized class. Strong covalent bonds make these minerals particularly stable chemically, and quartz is highly resistant. That toughness makes it a marker. A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz is the primary mineral that survived heavy weathering. The feldspars are the most abundant mineral group in the crust. In them, Al3+ takes the place of some Si4+, and added potassium, sodium or calcium balances the charge. Feldspars matter to soil for another reason: their weathering is a common source of the fine minerals in {{ref:soil-found-040}}.

soil-found-033.title: Phyllosilicates: minerals built in stacked sheets
soil-found-033.text: Some minerals split into thin, flexible flakes. These are the phyllosilicates, or sheet silicates, made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra. The class includes the micas and the minerals at the heart of {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Each tetrahedron is bound to its neighbors at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5. That leaves the tetrahedral sheet negatively charged, and a sheet of octahedra balances it. These tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers, and the stacking defines the groups. In 1:1 minerals, T-O stacks are held together by hydrogen bonds. In 2:1 minerals, T-O-T stacks are held by weaker van der Waals forces. Micas are also T-O-T stacks, with a difference. They put aluminum in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas the 1:1 and 2:1 minerals hold Al3+ in the octahedral sites. Metal ions bond mica layers together, making them harder. Because the bonds between layers are weak, phyllosilicates show a prominent basal cleavage, a tendency to split along flat planes. Octahedral sheets come in two kinds. When every site is filled they are trioctahedral. When some sites are empty, as in pyrophyllite, they are dioctahedral.

soil-found-040.title: Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil
soil-found-040.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE, which makes clay the longest-known ceramic raw material. Clay is a fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals, the hydrous aluminum sheet silicates described in {{ref:soil-found-033}}. Pure clay minerals are mostly white or pale. Impurities color natural clays, and small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones. Wet clay is plastic, and firing hardens it. In a field, clay is a mixed blessing. Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops. Yet they are more fertile, because they hold on to more positively charged nutrients. Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering. Mix sand, silt and less than 40% clay, and the result is {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Clay lasts in rock as well. Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common sedimentary rock.

soil-found-051.title: Soil texture: the sand, silt and clay recipe
soil-found-051.text: A soil's texture is the one trait farming cannot change. Soil texture is the quality of a soil set by its mix of sand, silt and clay particles. Only particles less than two millimeters across count. Texture classes rest on the percentages of the three. The USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes, and the UK-ADAS system uses 11. Texture can be judged by hand, as {{ref:soil-phys-049}} describes. It can also be measured quantitatively, for example with the method in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}, which is based on Stokes' law. Texture is fixed by a soil's mineral component, unlike the way its grains clump together. That permanence makes it useful. Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil, and predicts its response to drought and its lime needs. It also governs water. The amount of water best suited to plant growth rises as particles get finer, from sand to clay. The first texture classification, now called the international system, came in 1905 from {{ref:soil-hist-011}}.

soil-found-041.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay
soil-found-041.text: Granite carries the makings of clay. Its orthoclase feldspar weathers to {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions. Clay formation is the making of clay minerals, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into deposits. The work is done largely by acid hydrolysis. Weak carbonic acid in rainwater, or acid released by plant roots, breaks the bonds between aluminum and oxygen. Other metal ions and silica come loose, the silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid. Source rock and climate decide the product. Feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm, acid weathering, and {{ref:soil-chem-094}} under alkaline conditions. Igneous rock under alkaline conditions yields {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Intense weathering of other clay minerals produces an aluminum hydroxide. Hydrothermal activity can also make clay minerals locally. Then the clay may travel. Primary clays stay where they formed, as residual soil deposits. Secondary clays are carried off by flowing water and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

soil-found-044.title: Clay walls, brick and the barrier under a landfill
soil-found-044.text: Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population still live or work in buildings made with clay, often baked into brick. Clay is one of the oldest building materials on Earth. It served as mortar in brick chimneys and stone walls where protected from water. Because it is relatively impermeable, it also seals pond linings, dam cores and landfill barriers against toxic seepage. Early 21st-century studies have tested its absorption capacity for removing heavy metals from waste water and for purifying air.

soil-found-042.title: Kaolinite, smectite, illite: the main kinds of clay
soil-found-042.text: There are about 30 types of pure clay, but nature rarely serves one alone. Most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals. The main kinds of clay are grouped by their dominant clay minerals, each with its own entry later: {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. A few others, among them talc and pyrophyllite, are sometimes also classed as clay minerals. Chemical and physical tests struggle to tell them apart. X-ray diffraction identifies them most easily. One clay keeps a calendar. Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

soil-found-043.title: From Jōmon pots to pencil lead: clay at work
soil-found-043.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards come from central Honshu in Japan. Linked to the Jōmon culture, they date to around 14,000 BCE. People have shaped and fired clay ever since. Different clays, minerals and firing conditions produce earthenware, stoneware and porcelain. Ancient Mesopotamians inscribed cuneiform on clay tablets, the first known writing medium. Industry still relies on clay, in paper making, cement production and chemical filtering, and as a filler in pencil lead.

soil-found-060.title: Hydrolysis and carbonation, the acid attack on rock
soil-found-060.text: Weathering rock helps set how much carbon dioxide stays in the air. Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. The reactions behind it are hydrolysis and carbonation. In them, only part of a mineral dissolves, and the rest becomes a new solid, often one of the fine minerals of clay. Most is acid hydrolysis: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals. Carbonic acid, from dissolved carbon dioxide, is the main source of those protons, though organic acids also matter. The textbook case is orthoclase feldspar. With carbonic acid and water, it yields {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution. The weakest bonds between metal and oxygen go first. So igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, a sequence known as Bowen's reaction series. There are exceptions, such as silica, which is unusually unstable. Carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide. It can also turn primary minerals into the secondary minerals of {{ref:soil-found-034}}, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.

soil-found-064.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger
soil-found-064.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into clay minerals and iron oxides. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. Biotite then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay minerals and iron oxides. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

soil-found-039.title: Should minerals made by living things count?
soil-found-039.text: Over 60 biominerals had been named before the International Mineralogical Association drew up its listing, yet they are not on its official list. The IMA definition excludes crystalline substances made by living things, and mineralogists still disagree about that choice. In 1981, Lowenstam argued that organisms form a diverse array of minerals, some of which cannot form inorganically. In 2005, Skinner counted biominerals, created by organisms' metabolism, as minerals, and allowed a mineral to be crystalline or amorphous. The question touches soil directly. Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface. They can precipitate metals from solution and speed up mineral dissolution.

soil-found-034.title: Carbonate minerals and the geologist's acid test
soil-found-034.text: Field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid for a quick test. All carbonates react with acid, so a drop tells them apart from other minerals. Carbonate minerals are those whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−. The chief ones are calcite, aragonite and dolomite. Calcite, CaCO3, is the most common, and the main constituent of limestone and marble. Dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2. Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings. Weathering by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can also produce secondary carbonate minerals.

soil-found-038.title: Scratch, streak and shine: telling minerals apart
soil-found-038.text: Color is the most obvious thing about a mineral, and often not diagnostic at all. Mineral identification tells minerals apart by physical properties: crystal habit, hardness, luster, color, streak, cleavage and specific gravity. Hardness is usually measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond. The streak is the color of the powdered mineral, and trace elements and weathering do not change it. Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or X-ray diffraction analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming. Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that X-ray diffraction can determine.

soil-found-036.title: Sulfate minerals and the gypsum left by evaporation
soil-found-036.text: As saline water evaporates, minerals precipitate out of it. Sulfate minerals, which contain the sulfate anion [SO4]2−, commonly form this way, as evaporites. Gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, is by far the most common hydrous sulfate. It forms alongside other evaporites such as calcite and halite, and its anhydrous counterpart is anhydrite. Sulfates also occur in hydrothermal veins, or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.

soil-found-047.title: Organic matter that minerals keep for centuries
soil-found-047.text: Some carbon in soil lasts a few years; some lasts centuries. The difference often lies in what it is stuck to. Mineral-associated organic matter is soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces. It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules. They bond to charged mineral surfaces or are locked inside aggregates, crumbs of soil particles stuck together. Binding to minerals makes this carbon harder for decomposers to reach. So it resists microbial breakdown and stays in the soil's store of carbon. It typically persists for centuries. By contrast, {{ref:soil-bio-118}}, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

reviews.what-soil-is-made-of: Soil's solid matter arrives from two directions. From below, rock formed hot and under pressure meets the cool, wet surface, and physical, chemical and biological weathering take it apart. Feldspars and other silicates turn into clay minerals and iron oxides, while tough quartz survives as sand and silt. From above, plant debris decays into soil organic matter, and climate decides how much of it builds up. The two meet on clay and oxide surfaces, which bind organic molecules for centuries and help make soil a carbon store of an estimated 2,500 gigatons.
